findings.description: If the native setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/requestAnimationFrame returns undefined or null, `isNumber` is false and the else branch evaluates `handleOrId.refresh`, which throws a TypeError. The old code explicitly guarded against this case with 'check whether handle is null, because some polyfill or browser may return undefined'. The same crash applies to any non-numeric, non-object return value. Scheduling the timer now throws instead of returning the task.

When the native set function returns a non-number, the code reads `handleOrId.refresh` unguarded. Some polyfills and browsers return `undefined` or `null` from setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate or requestAnimationFrame, and the old code explicitly handled that. In those cases this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'refresh')` while scheduling, which is a regression.

The code that copied `handle.ref` and `handle.unref` onto the task (`task.ref` and `task.unref`) was removed. When a task is returned in place of the handle (non-Node or polyfilled environments), callers lose `ref`/`unref` support. This is an unrelated behaviour regression.

The comment edit changes "idents" to "indents". The regex documentation describes valid CSS identifiers, so "indents" is a wrong term and makes the comment misleading. Runtime behavior is not affected.

The template still passes `providers()` to `ng-injector-providers`, not the new `sortedProviders()`. The sorting that used to run when `latestInjectorProviders` arrived was removed from the message handler and moved into `sortedProviders`, which nothing uses. The providers list now shows in the order the backend sends it, which regresses the previous alphabetical-by-token order.

`init()` is now called inside `afterRenderEffect`, which re-runs on every `componentExplorerView` update. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` listener, so handlers accumulate and fire multiple times per message. Each run also calls `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer`, which clean up and recreate both visualizers. This resets the user's zoom, pan and selection on every refresh, and `init()` previously ran only once.

Tab visibility was switched from a `display:none` CSS class to the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements, and the `.hidden` rules were deleted. The `hidden` attribute only applies the UA default `display:none`. Any author style such as `:host {display:block/flex}` on these components overrides it, so inactive tabs can stay visible and stack on screen. The previous `ng-injector-tree.hidden` special case, which used `visibility:hidden` and absolute positioning so the tree could still be laid out and measured, is also gone.

`init()` is called inside `afterRenderEffect` on every `componentExplorerView` change. Each call registers another `highlightComponent` message-bus listener, so listeners accumulate and fire repeatedly. It also recreates both `InjectorTreeVisualizer`s each time, which discards the user's pan/zoom state and rebuilds the graph on every update. Previously the listeners were registered once and the visualizers were created once.

The template still passes the raw `providers()` to `ng-injector-providers` and checks `providers().length`. The new `sortedProviders` computed is never used, so the provider list is no longer sorted by token. This regresses the previous behavior, where providers were sorted before being set.

Tab visibility now relies on the `[hidden]` attribute instead of the `.hidden` class with `display:none`. The attribute only applies the user-agent `display:none`, which any author style such as `:host { display: block/flex }` on these components overrides. Inactive tabs may therefore stay visible and stack on screen. The old `ng-injector-tree.hidden` handling that kept the SVG measurable while hidden was also removed.

The single-file label `@npm//:node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js` was replaced by the whole `//:node_modules/zone.js` package target. The shell-browser `index.html` and any rules that copy or reference `zone.umd.min.js` by path were not updated in this diff. If they still expect the old layout (for example `./npm/node_modules/...`), the extension page will fail to load zone.js. The same applies to `devtools/src/BUILD.bazel`, where `devapp` now ships zone.js under a different path and `tslib.js` is no longer shipped, but `devtools/src/index.html` is unchanged.

The devapp now packages zone.js from `//:node_modules/zone.js`, so it lands at `node_modules/zone.js/...`, not the old `npm/node_modules/zone.js/...`. The same change updates demo-standalone's index.html, but no index.html for devtools/src or shell-browser is updated. If either still loads `./npm/node_modules/zone.js/bundles/zone.umd.min.js`, the script returns 404 and zone.js never loads, so the app fails at runtime. The removed tslib.js is also no longer shipped, which would break any page still referencing it.

The new call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` runs for every `__`-separated name resolved by attribute traversal. That includes non-field attributes on the related object, such as a property, method or annotation (e.g. `list_display = ['parent__some_property']`). `get_fields_from_path` resolves each segment with `_meta.get_field`, so it raises `FieldDoesNotExist` (or `NotRelationField`) for those names. `lookup_field` previously returned the value via `getattr` traversal. The exception is raised inside the `except` handler and not caught, so the changelist crashes instead of rendering the value. The call needs a try/except that falls back to `f = None`.

lookup_field() now returns the final field `f` for any `a__b` path. Callers such as `items_for_result` treat a non-None `f` as a model field of the row object. For a path ending in a ForeignKey (e.g. `parent__parent`), `f.remote_field` is a ManyToOneRel, so the changelist runs `getattr(result, f.name)` with only the last segment. That returns the wrong object (the row's own `parent`) instead of the traversed value. It also adds an unguarded `get_fields_from_path()` call, which can raise NotRelationField or FieldDoesNotExist in cases where the plain getattr traversal worked, such as a path ending in a property or a custom attribute. That would crash the changelist instead of rendering the value.

Converting the term with `formfield.to_python(bit)` can return `None` for an empty term, such as a quoted `""` search. Form fields return `None` for empty values, and `field__exact=None` becomes `IS NULL`. A search for an empty string on an integer, date or similar `__exact` field would then match every row where that field is NULL, instead of skipping the lookup as invalid. Related-field `__exact` lookups also build a `ModelChoiceField` and query the database once per search term, which adds queries.

The search term is converted with `formfield().to_python()`, which is too permissive for some fields. `forms.BooleanField.to_python` returns True for any string except 'false', 'False' and '0'. A `bool__exact` search for 'foo' therefore becomes `bool__exact=True` and matches every True row. Previously the cast-to-string comparison matched nothing. Other form fields that normalise arbitrary input behave the same way. The converted value is also used instead of the raw term, so the query semantics change silently.

When an `fk__exact` search field is used, `prev_field` is the ForeignKey, so `formfield()` is a ModelChoiceField. Its `to_python` runs a database `queryset.get(pk=bit)` for every term and every such lookup during validation. This adds extra queries on every changelist search. The converted value is a model instance that is passed to the filter, and a term that matches no related row is dropped rather than searched. Validation here is meant to be cheap and side-effect free.

The rewritten wrap() does not preserve blank lines or trailing newlines. For each line from splitlines(True), TextWrapper.wrap() turns '
' into a space and drops it as whitespace, so a blank line returns [] and disappears. A trailing newline is also stripped by the final '
'.join. As a result, paragraph breaks ('a

b') collapse to 'a
b' and a trailing '
' is lost. This regresses the old behavior of wordwrap and wrap() for existing users.

The rewrite changes behaviour for blank lines and trailing newlines. Each line from splitlines(True) goes through TextWrapper.wrap, which turns the newline into a space and then drops it. A blank line such as the one in "a

b" therefore yields an empty list and disappears, so paragraph breaks are collapsed. A trailing newline is also lost, because the lines are joined with "
" and there is no final separator. The old implementation preserved both, so this is a regression for existing wordwrap users.

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals and ordinary text, not just variable lookups. For a literal such as `{{ "Wait..." }}`, `{{ "a..b"|upper }}` or `{{ _("loading...") }}`, `FilterExpression.var` is the literal string (or a Variable wrapping it), and its text contains `..`. These templates have no double-dot lookup, yet they now emit a RemovedInDjango70Warning. When the deprecation ends and the warning becomes an error, they would raise TemplateSyntaxError. The check should apply only to non-literal Variable lookups, such as the `lookups` of a Variable.

The warning message reads `self.origin.name` without a guard. `Parser.origin` can be None when a Parser is built directly, as some code and tests do, so a `..` in a variable raises AttributeError instead of a warning. Template compilation normally sets an origin, so this only affects direct Parser use.

The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals and translated literals, not just variable lookups. For `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ _("Wait...") }}`, `FilterExpression.var` is the literal string or a Variable whose `str()` is the original text, and either contains `..`. These templates now emit a RemovedInDjango70Warning. Once the deprecation ends and the warning becomes an error, they would raise TemplateSyntaxError. The check should only apply to real variable lookups, for example when `var` is a Variable with `lookups` set and one of the lookups is empty.

The prefetch filter is now always a TupleIn over ColPairs keyed on queryset.model._meta.db_table, including the common single-column FK case. Single-column prefetches used to produce a plain `col IN (...)`. They now go through tuple-lookup SQL or its OR fallback, and None values in instances_dict keys are no longer dropped as In did. Hard-coding the model's db_table as the alias is also wrong if the foreign-related field lives on a parent table (multi-table inheritance, to_field on an inherited field) or the queryset uses a different alias. The old `field__in` lookup resolved the join and alias correctly in those cases. The result is a possible regression in SQL shape and correctness.

`docutils.core.publish_parts` has no string-valued `writer` argument. `writer` expects a Writer instance and `writer_name` is the string argument. Passing `writer="html"` makes docutils treat the string as the writer object, and `set_components` will not apply the default writer name. Later steps that use writer attributes such as `settings_spec`, `translate` and `parts` then fail with AttributeError on `str`. Also, `writer_name` falls back to the default `pseudoxml`, so even if the call did not crash, the output would not be HTML. This breaks all admindocs RST rendering.

The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the raw '-' prefix for descending fields (e.g. '-name'). The original code used `fields_orders`, which strips it. A valid index like `Index(fields=['-name'])` now reports a bogus models.E012 error saying it refers to the nonexistent field '-name'. It should use the stripped field names from `fields_orders`.

The local-field check (E012, E013, E016 and similar) now runs inside the per-database loop in `_check_indexes`. If `databases` is empty or None, or the router disallows migration, these errors are never reported. With multiple databases they are reported once per database. Previously they ran once regardless of databases, which is why many tests had to be changed to pass `databases=`. Passing a set also makes the order of the resulting errors nondeterministic.

The feature-warning checks (W037, W040, W043) were moved into the per-index method but still scan all of `model._meta.indexes`. W037 even tests `self.condition` inside a generator over unrelated indexes. As a result, W040 and W043 are emitted for every index in the model if any one index uses the unsupported feature, even for indexes that don't use it. A model with N indexes produces N duplicate warnings instead of one, which is a behavior regression.

Index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop, and only for databases that allow migrating the model. Name checks (E033/E034) and field checks (E012-style `indexes` errors) used to run unconditionally. With `Model.check()` and no databases, or a model that no database allows migrating, these errors are silently dropped. The existing tests had to be changed to pass `databases=` to keep passing. With several databases, the same name and field errors are reported once per database.

The feature warnings W037, W040 and W043 still scan `model._meta.indexes` (`any(index.include for index in model._meta.indexes)`). Now that `check()` runs once per index, every index on the model emits the warning if any one index uses the feature. A model with N indexes and one covering index gets N duplicate W040 warnings, and likewise for W043. W037 uses `self.condition` inside a generator over `index`, so it ignores the loop variable. This is a regression from the previous single warning per database.

The code now reads `window.relatedWindows`, but the file declares `relatedWindows` as a block-scoped `const` (`const relatedWindows = []`). It is not a property of `window`, and `showRelatedObjectPopup` pushes windows onto the local const. In production `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` therefore throws a TypeError on `.indexOf`, after the value is set but before `win.close()`. Raw-id lookup popups would no longer close or clean up. The new tests only pass because they create `window.relatedWindows` themselves. The fix should have kept using the local `relatedWindows` or exposed it deliberately.

`relatedWindows` is a local `const` inside the IIFE in RelatedObjectLookups.js and is never exported to `window`. Changing it to `window.relatedWindows` makes `window.relatedWindows` undefined in real admin pages. The next call to `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'indexOf')`. This happens after the value is set but before `win.close()`, so the popup never closes and the window is never removed from the real tracking array. The new test hides this by setting `window.relatedWindows = window.relatedWindows || []` in `beforeEach`. The original unqualified reference is correct and should be restored.

In the insert path, `returning_fields` starts as `list(meta.db_returning_fields)`. A field that is already in it (a `db_default` field on backends that support RETURNING) is appended again when its value has `resolve_expression`. That always holds for the `DatabaseDefault` placeholder, and also when the user assigns an expression. The field then appears twice in the RETURNING clause and in `returning_fields`. The returned columns no longer line up with the intended fields, and `_assign_returned_values` assigns the wrong values or does so redundantly. This is a regression for every model with a `db_default` on SQLite, PostgreSQL and Oracle. An `if field not in returning_fields` guard is missing.

In the insert path, a field that is already in `meta.db_returning_fields` is appended to `returning_fields` again whenever its value has `resolve_expression`. A field with a `db_default` is the main case, because its attribute holds a `DatabaseDefault` expression and `field.db_returning` is true. The upstream version guards this with `if field not in returning_fields`, but this diff does not. The field then appears twice in the RETURNING clause, producing duplicate columns. `_assign_returned_values` zips the returned values against the longer list, so the field is assigned twice and the returned columns no longer line up with `returning_fields`.

get_supported_language_variant() now raises ValueError for over-long codes (strict=True, or non-strict with no hyphen). Existing callers only catch LookupError. get_language_from_request() reads the language cookie and passes it in without a length check. get_language_from_path() passes a regex-matched path segment with strict=True, and that regex has no length limit. A request with a cookie or URL prefix longer than 500 characters (for example 'xxxx…') would therefore make LocaleMiddleware or get_language_from_request raise an uncaught ValueError and return a 500, where it previously fell back to the default language or a 404.

The UNNEST path builds placeholders as a plain `(%s)::<db_type>[]` for every field. It ignores any custom `field.get_placeholder()` or `get_db_prep_save()` placeholder logic that the base `assemble_as_sql` applies. Fields that rely on such placeholders (for example GIS geometry fields, or custom fields with their own placeholder) get a bare cast instead of their custom SQL. Values that cannot be cast through an array literal, such as adapter-wrapped values, can also make a previously working multi-row `bulk_create()` fail on PostgreSQL. Only arrays and `as_sql` values are excluded from the optimization.

The UNNEST path skips the per-field placeholders that the base assemble_as_sql applies via get_placeholder(). A field that defines get_placeholder, such as PostGIS geometry fields, normally wraps its value in a SQL function like ST_GeomFromEWKB(%s). Here the value is cast straight to db_type[] instead. Because PostGIS operations inherit from the PostgreSQL operations and so pick up this compiler, bulk_create with two or more rows can generate wrong or failing SQL. The condition at line 31 only excludes compilable values and array fields, and does not check for custom placeholders.

Only attachments added through attach() become EmailAttachment named tuples. Attachments passed to the EmailMessage constructor (attachments=[(filename, content, mimetype)]) are not converted, so they stay plain tuples. Code that accesses msg.attachments[i].filename or .content then raises AttributeError for constructor-supplied attachments, which contradicts the new docs. A 2-tuple passed to the constructor also stays a 2-tuple, so the attributes are inconsistent. The constructor should route attachments through attach().

_create_alternatives now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`. Existing code that appends plain tuples to `msg.alternatives`, or assigns a list of tuples to it after construction, previously worked. It now raises AttributeError when the message is built, because plain tuples have no such attributes. This breaks backward compatibility. The old code unpacked positionally with `*alternative`.

The namedtuple typename is "Attachment" but the module-level name is `EmailAttachment`. Pickling or deepcopying an EmailMessage that has attachments fails, because pickle looks up `django.core.mail.message.Attachment`, which does not exist. Plain tuples pickled fine before, so this is a regression for anyone who pickles messages, for example when queueing them.

The keyword-only `single_object` parameter is removed from the public `LogEntryManager.log_actions()`. Any caller that already passes `single_object=True` (the parameter existed in released 5.1 versions) will now get a `TypeError`. That is a compatibility break in a patch-release regression fix. Also, the return type now depends on the length of the input: a single `LogEntry` instance for one object, a list for any other count. A one-item queryset therefore behaves differently from an N-item one.

The form field passes `max_length=self.max_length` into `clean_ipv6_address`. `kwargs.setdefault` does not replace an explicit `max_length=None`, so a caller who sets that to remove the length limit leaves `self.max_length` as None. Any IPv6 value containing ':' then reaches `len(ip_str) > None` in `_ipv6_address_from_str`, which raises TypeError (a 500 error) instead of validating or returning a ValidationError. This is a regression for existing code that passes `max_length=None`.

The SelectBox cache guard tests `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` but then updates the cache for `select.id`. The guard should be about the target select. If a popup is added from a plain FK select, `currentSelect` has no cache entry, so the guard is true for every other related select. For a plain FK select that is also an `available-source` target, `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, ...)` dereferences an undefined `SelectBox.cache[select.id]` and throws a TypeError. That aborts the forEach, so the remaining selects are not updated. In the opposite case, an add from the m2m popup passes `toElem`, whose cache exists, so the guard is false and the filter-widget cache is never updated for other m2m widgets. They will show the new option until they redisplay, and then it disappears.

The cache guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` but the cache update targets `select.id`. When the change comes from an M2M "+" popup, `currentSelect` is the `_to` box, which always has a cache entry, so the condition is false. The new option is therefore never added to the SelectBox cache of other related filter-horizontal "from" boxes. Those boxes show it in the DOM, but a later `redisplay`, filter or move operation drops it or fails to move it. When `currentSelect` is a plain select with no cache entry, the condition is true and `add_to_cache` runs for `select.id`. If `select.id` has no cache entry either, that call throws a TypeError. The guard should check `select.id`.

MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message() applies `% self.min_length` to the ngettext msgids before translation lookup. The lookup keys become literal strings such as "...at least 8 characters." instead of the catalog's "...%(min_length)d character(s).", so existing translations no longer match. Users with a non-English language will see the English message. The `min_length` entry in ValidationError params was also dropped, which regresses existing behavior for code that reads `params`.

MinimumLengthValidator now interpolates min_length into the msgid before calling ngettext ("... %d character." % self.min_length). The gettext lookup therefore uses strings such as "...at least 8 characters.", which are not in any translation catalog. The existing catalogs use the msgid with %(min_length)d, and the string extractor sees a different, non-literal msgid. The too-short error is therefore never translated and always appears in English, a regression for non-English users. The change also drops params={"min_length": ...} from the ValidationError, so code that inspects error.params loses the value.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match. Renaming `Order` would also match content types such as `orderitem` or `preorder` in the same app. Permissions of unrelated models would then be renamed to `*_neworder`, and the match should be exact.

Every permission on the matching content types is rewritten to `<prefix>_<newmodel>` with a default name, where the prefix is `codename.split('_')[0]`. Custom permissions (for example `can_export_oldmodel`, or any with a custom name or verbose_name) are collapsed into `can_newmodel` or overwritten. Custom permission names are lost, and several custom permissions can collide with each other. Only the four default permissions should be renamed.

The operation ignores the target database alias. `Permission.objects.filter` and `permission.save()` do not use `using=db`, and the ContentType queryset is not bound to the alias either. With multiple databases, migrating a non-default database reads and writes the wrong one. The router may also direct the writes elsewhere.

`IntegrityError` is silently swallowed on a codename conflict. The old permission is left behind and still points at the old codename, with no warning. Users who hold that permission keep it under a stale codename instead of the renamed one.

The auth handler inserts `RenamePermission` directly after `RenameModel`, which puts it before the `RenameContentType` operation that contenttypes inserted. Backward migration runs operations in reverse, so `RenameContentType` reverts first. The content type then already has the old model name, but `rename_backward` filters on the new model name, so it can match nothing and permissions would not be restored.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match rather than an exact match. Renaming `User` to `Member` also matches content types such as `userprofile` and `superuser`. All permissions on those unrelated models are then renamed to `*_member`, corrupting their codenames and names. The lookup should be `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is rewritten using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix. A custom permission like `can_publish_article` becomes `can_newmodel` with the name 'Can can new model'. Several custom permissions on one model collapse to the same codename, so only the first rename succeeds and the rest are silently dropped by the IntegrityError handler. Custom permissions are therefore lost or corrupted. The new name also ignores the model's `verbose_name`, overwriting any customized permission names.

The MRO loop collects a name if any class in the MRO defines it as a property. It ignores whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property, such as a model field, a plain attribute or a method. The old `inspect.getattr_static` lookup returned only the most-derived attribute, so those names were excluded. Now a name like `foo` can appear in `_property_names` even though `Child.foo` is a field or a regular attribute. `Model.__init__` and `_extract_model_params` use this set to treat kwargs as property setters, so they can call `setattr` on the wrong thing or skip field validation. This is a regression. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

The new MRO loop adds every property found in any class's __dict__ and never checks whether a more-derived class overrides that name with a non-property. The old getattr_static approach resolved the name to the first MRO match, so it did not report such names. For example, a subclass (or abstract-base child) can replace an inherited property with a model field or plain attribute. That name is still reported as a property here. This affects Model.__init__, which treats property names as settable kwargs, and the get_or_create/update_or_create defaults handling. It also affects the pk-property check. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and skip them.

The NotSupportedError guard only fires when `self.rhs` is a bare `Query`. `Subquery.resolve_expression` returns `ExpressionWrapper(resolved.query, ...)` when an explicit `output_field` differs from the query's own, so `pk__gt=Subquery(..., output_field=...)` bypasses the check. On Oracle it then produces unsupported tuple-vs-subquery SQL and fails with a database error instead of the intended NotSupportedError. This is a narrow edge case.
